# Chapter 10 — Training linear models

```{python}
#| include: false
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
GARNET, GREY, BLUE, SEED = "#881124", "#8c8c8c", "#1f77b4", 368
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 3.6), "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 11})
def usd(x):
    return f"{x:,.0f}"
def rmse(y, yhat):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(y) - np.asarray(yhat)) ** 2)))

URL = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/"
       "main/data/2022/2022-07-05/rent.csv")
path = Path("../data/rent.csv")
if not path.exists():
    path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    pd.read_csv(URL).to_csv(path, index=False)
rent = pd.read_csv(path)
d = (rent.dropna(subset=["beds", "sqft", "county"])
         .query("room_in_apt == 0 and beds <= 5 and 200 <= sqft <= 5000 and 500 <= price <= 15000")
         .assign(log_price=lambda x: np.log(x["price"])))
train, test = train_test_split(d, test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED)   # the same rows as Chapter 9
```

> **The question:** a housing office has to set a voucher for a flat nobody has advertised yet. What rent should it expect, in dollars, and how wide a range should it be ready for?

## OLS as a predictor

```{python}
#| include: false
FORMULA = "log_price ~ np.log(sqft) + C(beds) + C(county) + C(year)"
fit = smf.ols(FORMULA, data=train).fit()
elast = fit.params["np.log(sqft)"]
rmse_log = rmse(test["log_price"], fit.predict(test))
rmse_log_train = rmse(train["log_price"], fit.predict(train))
```

You have met ordinary least squares as an **estimator**. In econometrics the point of a regression is the coefficient, and the questions you ask of it are about the coefficient: is it unbiased, is it consistent, what is its standard error, have I left out a variable that is correlated with both $x$ and $y$?

In this chapter the same machine does a different job. OLS is a **predictor**: a rule that takes the features of a flat and returns a guess of its rent. The questions change. Nobody asks whether the coefficient on square footage is causal. We ask how far off the guesses are on flats the model has never seen, and we answer with the test RMSE from Chapter 9.

Here is the model I will build on for most of the chapter. It is a regression of **log** rent on log square footage, with dummies for the number of bedrooms, the county and the year, fitted to the `{python} f"{len(train):,}"` training listings from Chapter 9 (the same cleaning, the same split):

```python
fit = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(sqft) + C(beds) + C(county) + C(year)", data=train).fit()
```

Its test RMSE is `{python} f"{rmse_log:.3f}"` log points, so a typical miss is roughly `{python} f"{rmse_log:.0%}"` of the rent. The training RMSE is `{python} f"{rmse_log_train:.3f}"`. The two are almost identical, which is what you expect from a model with `{python} len(fit.params)` coefficients and tens of thousands of rows: there is not enough flexibility to memorise anything. Why logs, and how to get back to dollars, is a section of its own below.

The coefficient on log square footage is `{python} f"{elast:.2f}"`. Read as an elasticity, a flat that is 10% bigger rents for about `{python} f"{10 * elast:.0f}"`% more. As a predictor, that is all it needs to be: a weight that, combined with the others, makes good guesses.

Why is OLS a sensible predictor even when the "true" model is surely not a straight line in these variables? Because of what OLS does: it picks the coefficients that make the squared errors in the training data as small as possible. If the world is not linear, OLS still gives the best *linear* approximation to it, in the sense of the smallest average squared error. That is exactly the loss we chose in Chapter 9. You do not need to believe the model to use it; you need it to predict well, and you check that on test data.

> An estimator is judged by whether $\hat\beta$ is close to $\beta$. A predictor is judged by whether $\hat y$ is close to $y$, on data it has not seen. Same arithmetic, different exam.

### Worked example — the omitted variable that does not matter

A colleague points out that the rent model leaves out the age of the building, the view, and whether there is parking. "Your coefficient on size is biased," she says. "Bigger flats are in newer buildings." Is she right, and should the housing office care?

### Solution

She is right about the coefficient. Bigger flats differ from smaller ones in many ways that also raise rent, so `{python} f"{elast:.2f}"` mixes the value of space with the value of everything that comes with space. As an estimate of what an extra square foot is *worth*, holding the flat otherwise fixed, it is biased.

For the housing office it barely matters. The office wants a good guess of the rent of a flat drawn from the same market. If bigger flats tend to come with parking, the size coefficient quietly absorbs some of the value of parking, and the prediction for a big flat is better for it, not worse. Omitted variables make predictions *noisier* (the variation they would explain ends up in the error), but they do not bias them, as long as the relationship between what is in the model and what is left out stays the same.

That last clause is the catch. If the city starts building large flats without parking, the relationship changes and the predictions go wrong, and nothing in the test RMSE, computed on old listings, would have warned you. Prediction models assume that tomorrow looks like the training data.

## The normal equation, in words

```{python}
#| include: false
import patsy
yv, Xd = patsy.dmatrices(FORMULA, train, return_type="dataframe")
X_np, y_np = Xd.to_numpy(), yv.to_numpy().ravel()
beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(X_np.T @ X_np, X_np.T @ y_np)
max_gap = np.abs(beta_hat - fit.params.to_numpy()).max()
```

How does the computer find the OLS coefficients? For linear regression there is a formula, the **normal equation**:

$$\hat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'y$$

where $X$ is the table of features, one row per flat and one column per feature (plus a column of ones for the intercept), and $y$ is the column of log rents.

I do not want you to memorise the matrix algebra. I want you to be able to say what it does, in words:

- $X'y$ measures how much each feature moves with rent. Size moves with rent a lot; the year dummies a bit.
- $X'X$ measures how much the features move with *each other*. Size moves with bedrooms; San Francisco moves with small flats.
- Multiplying by the inverse of $X'X$ **untangles** the two. It credits each feature with the part of its co-movement with rent that the other features cannot account for. That is the "holding the others constant" you learned in econometrics, done in one step.

In numpy it is two lines. `patsy` turns the formula into the matrix $X$, exactly as `statsmodels` does behind the scenes:

```python
yv, Xd = patsy.dmatrices("log_price ~ np.log(sqft) + C(beds) + C(county) + C(year)", train)
beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(Xd.T @ Xd, Xd.T @ yv)
```

The `{python} len(beta_hat)` coefficients agree with `statsmodels` to within `{python} f"{max_gap:.0e}"`, which is rounding error.

The normal equation is exact and, for a problem this size, instant. Its weakness is cost as the number of features grows. Computing it means working with $X'X$, a square table with one row and one column per feature, and the work of solving it grows roughly with the *cube* of the number of features. Double the rows and the job takes about twice as long. Double the features and it takes about eight times as long. With `{python} X_np.shape[1]` columns nobody notices. With the hundred thousand word counts of a text regression (Chapter 19), or data too big to fit in memory at once, you need another way. That way is gradient descent.

### Worked example — the normal equation with one feature

Three hypothetical flats have (centred) log sizes $x = -1, 0, 1$ and log rents $y = 7.0, 7.5, 8.2$. With one feature and an intercept, and $x$ centred at zero, the normal equation reduces to two familiar formulas. What are they, and what are the coefficients?

### Solution

When $x$ has mean zero, the intercept and the slope untangle completely, and the normal equation becomes

$$\hat\beta_0 = \bar y, \qquad \hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}.$$

The intercept is the mean log rent, $(7.0 + 7.5 + 8.2)/3 = 7.567$. The slope is $(-7.0 + 0 + 8.2)/(1 + 0 + 1) = 1.2/2 = 0.6$. The top of the slope formula is the "how much does $x$ move with $y$" part; the bottom is the "how much does $x$ move with itself" part. With more features, the bottom becomes the whole table $X'X$, but the idea is the same.

## Gradient descent

Gradient descent is how almost every model after this chapter is trained, from LASSO in Chapter 11 to the neural networks of Chapter 18. It is worth seeing it once on a problem where we know the right answer.

The idea is to forget the formula and walk downhill. The training MSE is a function of the coefficients: pick some $\beta$, and you get some average squared error. Picture that function as a landscape. For linear regression it is a bowl with a single lowest point, which is the OLS solution. Gradient descent starts somewhere (all zeros will do), works out which direction is downhill, takes a step that way, and repeats.

"Which direction is downhill" is the **gradient**, the vector of slopes of the MSE with respect to each coefficient. For the MSE of a linear model it is

$$\nabla \text{MSE}(\beta) = \frac{2}{n}X'(X\beta - y).$$

Read it from the inside out. $X\beta - y$ is the column of current errors. $X'$ times the errors asks, for each feature, whether the errors are large where that feature is large. If they are, that coefficient is too big and the gradient says so. Each step moves $\beta$ a little against the gradient:

$$\beta \leftarrow \beta - \eta\, \nabla \text{MSE}(\beta),$$

where $\eta$ (eta) is the **learning rate**, the size of the step. It is a hyperparameter, like $k$ in nearest neighbours.

Here it is in numpy, on a small version of the rent model with three standardised features (log size, bedrooms, year) so the numbers are easy to look at:

```{python}
cols = ["sqft", "beds", "year"]
Z = train[cols].assign(sqft=np.log(train["sqft"]))
Z = ((Z - Z.mean()) / Z.std()).to_numpy()
X3 = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])          # intercept + 3 standardised features
y3 = train["log_price"].to_numpy()

def batch_gd(eta, steps=200):
    b, path = np.zeros(X3.shape[1]), []
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = X3 @ b - y3
        b = b - eta * 2 / len(y3) * X3.T @ err         # one step downhill
        path.append(np.mean(err ** 2))
    return b, path
```

```{python}
#| include: false
b_exact = np.linalg.lstsq(X3, y3, rcond=None)[0]
H = 2 / len(y3) * X3.T @ X3
eta_max = 2 / np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).max()
etas = [0.01, 0.3, round(1.05 * eta_max, 2)]
runs = {eta: batch_gd(eta) for eta in etas}
b_good = runs[0.3][0]
gap_good = np.abs(b_good - b_exact).max()
gap_slow = np.abs(runs[0.01][0] - b_exact).max()
```

After 200 steps with $\eta = 0.3$, the coefficients agree with the normal equation to within `{python} f"{gap_good:.0e}"`. With $\eta = 0.01$ they are still off by up to `{python} f"{gap_slow:.2f}"`. With $\eta =$ `{python} f"{etas[2]:.2f}"` they never arrive at all:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Training MSE at each step of batch gradient descent, for three learning rates."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for eta, c, lab in zip(etas, [GREY, GARNET, BLUE], ["too small", "about right", "too big"]):
    ax.plot(runs[eta][1], color=c, lw=2.2, label=f"η = {eta} ({lab})")
ax.axhline(np.mean((X3 @ b_exact - y3) ** 2), color="black", ls=":", lw=1, label="OLS minimum")
ax.set(yscale="log", ylim=(0.05, 200), xlabel="Step", ylabel="Training MSE (log scale)",
       title="The learning rate decides whether you arrive")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9); plt.show()
```

That picture is the **learning-rate trade-off**. Too small, and every step is safe but you need thousands of them. Too big, and each step overshoots the bottom of the bowl, lands higher up the other side, and the next step overshoots further: the error explodes. The best learning rate is as large as possible without overshooting.

Standardising the features matters here, as it did for nearest neighbours. If square footage were left in raw units (hundreds to thousands) next to bedrooms (one to five), the bowl would be a long narrow valley: steep across the square-footage direction and nearly flat along the bedrooms direction. Any step size small enough not to overshoot in the steep direction would crawl in the flat one.

### Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent

```{python}
#| include: false
def minibatch_gd(eta=0.02, batch=64, epochs=5, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    b = np.zeros(X3.shape[1])
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in np.array_split(rng.permutation(len(y3)), len(y3) // batch):
            Xb, yb = X3[idx], y3[idx]
            b = b - eta * 2 / len(yb) * Xb.T @ (Xb @ b - yb)
    return b
b_mb = minibatch_gd()
gap_mb = np.abs(b_mb - b_exact).max()
n_updates = 5 * (len(y3) // 64)
```

**Batch** gradient descent, the version above, uses every training row to compute each step. With `{python} f"{len(y3):,}"` rows that is fine; with a billion it is not. Two cheaper versions look at fewer rows per step.

- **Stochastic gradient descent** (SGD) computes the gradient from *one* randomly chosen row and steps. Each step is noisy (one flat is a poor guide to the whole market), but steps are so cheap that you can take millions of them. The path to the bottom staggers rather than glides, and it never quite settles: near the minimum it keeps bouncing around. The usual fix is to shrink the learning rate over time.
- **Mini-batch** gradient descent is the compromise everyone actually uses: a random batch of, say, 64 rows per step. Much less noisy than one row, much cheaper than all of them, and it suits the way computer hardware likes to do arithmetic.

One full pass through the training data is called an **epoch**. Five epochs of mini-batches of 64 rows is `{python} f"{n_updates:,}"` small steps, and it lands within `{python} f"{gap_mb:.3f}"` of the exact coefficients. scikit-learn's `SGDRegressor` does the same with more care about the learning rate.

For linear regression on data that fit in memory, none of this beats the normal equation, and `LinearRegression` does not use it. The point is that gradient descent works for *any* loss you can take slopes of, with or without a formula, which is why you will see it again in Chapter 11 (as a form of regularisation) and in Chapter 18 (as the only way to train a neural network).

### Worked example — how big a step?

For a linear model, there is a largest learning rate beyond which batch gradient descent explodes. It depends on how steep the bowl is in its steepest direction. For our three-feature model that limit is `{python} f"{eta_max:.3f}"`. Our "too big" rate was `{python} f"{etas[2]:.2f}"`, only 5% over the limit. Why does such a small excess make the error explode rather than merely slow things down?

### Solution

Because overshooting compounds. In the steepest direction, a step at the limit lands exactly as far past the bottom as it started, on the other side; it bounces forever without getting closer. A step slightly over the limit lands slightly *further* away than it started, every time. After one step you are 5% further from the bottom along that direction, after two steps about 10%, and after 200 steps about $1.05^{200} \approx$ `{python} f"{1.05 ** 200:,.0f}"` times as far. That is why the blue line in the figure first drops, as the gentler directions still improve, and then climbs steadily once the one runaway direction takes over. Learning rates fail fast and visibly, which is a mercy: if your training loss is rising, halve $\eta$ before you suspect anything else.

## Logs, and getting back to dollars

```{python}
#| include: false
fit_lev = smf.ols("price ~ sqft + C(beds) + C(county) + C(year)", data=train).fit()
smear = float(np.mean(np.exp(fit.resid)))
pred_naive = np.exp(fit.predict(test))
pred_smear = smear * pred_naive
pred_lev = fit_lev.predict(test)
r_lev, r_naive, r_smear = rmse(test["price"], pred_lev), rmse(test["price"], pred_naive), rmse(test["price"], pred_smear)
normal_factor = float(np.exp(fit.scale / 2))
```

Chapter 9 predicted rent in dollars. This chapter has been predicting **log** rent. There are three reasons to prefer logs for prices, wages and incomes, and you have met them all in econometrics.

- **Effects are proportional.** A bigger flat rents for a certain *percentage* more, not a fixed number of dollars more, whether it is in Vallejo or in Pacific Heights.
- **The skew goes away.** Rents have a long right tail; log rents are close to symmetric. A squared-error loss in dollars lets the few very expensive flats dominate the fit.
- **The errors are more even.** In dollars, a model misses expensive flats by much more than cheap ones (the residual plot fans out). In logs the misses are similar in size across the range.

But the housing office pays vouchers in dollars, so at some point we must turn a predicted log rent back into rent. The obvious move is to take the exponential, $e^{\widehat{\log y}}$. It is wrong in a predictable direction.

The reason is that the exponential of an average is not the average of the exponential. The regression predicts the *mean of log rent* for flats like this one. Exponentiating gives (roughly) the *median* rent of those flats, and with a right skew the mean rent is above the median. So naive predictions come in too low on average. On the test set the average actual rent is \$`{python} usd(test["price"].mean())`; the average naive prediction is \$`{python} usd(pred_naive.mean())`.

The fix is due to Duan (1983) and is called the **smearing** estimator. Multiply every naive prediction by one number, the average of $e^{\text{residual}}$ over the training data:

$$\hat y_{\text{dollars}} = e^{\widehat{\log y}} \times \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\hat\varepsilon_i}$$

```python
smear = np.mean(np.exp(fit.resid))
pred_dollars = smear * np.exp(fit.predict(test))
```

Here the factor is `{python} f"{smear:.4f}"`, which lifts the average test prediction to \$`{python} usd(pred_smear.mean())`, close to the actual average. Now we can compare the log model with a model fitted directly in dollars, both scored in dollars on the test set:

| Model | Test RMSE, \$ a month |
|---|---|
| Rent in dollars on square feet, bedrooms, county, year | \$`{python} usd(r_lev)` |
| Log rent, naive $e^{\hat y}$ | \$`{python} usd(r_naive)` |
| Log rent, with smearing | \$`{python} usd(r_smear)` |

The log model wins even when judged in dollars, and smearing helps a little more. The bigger gain from smearing is not in the RMSE but in the *total*: a voucher budget built from naive predictions would come up `{python} f"{1 - pred_naive.mean() / test['price'].mean():.1%}"` short.

### Worked example — reading a log RMSE and a smearing factor

**(a)** The test RMSE of the log model is `{python} f"{rmse_log:.3f}"`. Explain to the housing office what that means in plain words. **(b)** If the errors were normally distributed with variance $\sigma^2$, the right correction factor would be $e^{\sigma^2/2}$. Compute it from the regression and compare it with the smearing factor.

### Solution

**(a)** A miss of 0.25 in log rent is a miss of about 25% of the rent (more exactly, $e^{0.25} - 1 \approx 28\%$ too high, or $1 - e^{-0.25} \approx 22\%$ too low). So "a typical estimate is off by about a quarter of the rent, in one direction or the other". A percentage is a more honest summary than a dollar figure here, because the size of the miss scales with the rent.

**(b)** The regression's residual variance is `{python} f"{fit.scale:.4f}"`, so $e^{\sigma^2/2} =$ `{python} f"{normal_factor:.4f}"`, against a smearing factor of `{python} f"{smear:.4f}"`. They are close but not equal. Smearing does not assume normal errors; it uses the actual residuals, whatever their shape. That is why I use it by default.

## Interactions

```{python}
#| include: false
fit_int = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(sqft) * C(county) + C(beds) + C(year)", data=train).fit()
counties = sorted(train["county"].unique())
el = {c: fit_int.params["np.log(sqft)"] + fit_int.params.get(f"np.log(sqft):C(county)[T.{c}]", 0.0) for c in counties}
el = pd.Series(el).sort_values()
rmse_int = rmse(test["log_price"], fit_int.predict(test))
lo_c, hi_c = el.index[0], el.index[-1]
```

The model so far says that a 10% bigger flat rents for about `{python} f"{10 * elast:.0f}"`% more everywhere in the Bay Area. Is that plausible? Space might be worth more where land is scarce, or less where every flat is already big.

An **interaction** lets one feature's slope depend on another. In a formula, `np.log(sqft) * C(county)` means: the log-size slope, the county dummies, *and* a separate log-size slope for each county.

```python
fit_int = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(sqft) * C(county) + C(beds) + C(year)", data=train).fit()
```

The implied elasticity of rent with respect to size, county by county:

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(el.round(2).to_string())
```

They range from `{python} f"{el.iloc[0]:.2f}"` in `{python} lo_c.title()` to `{python} f"{el.iloc[-1]:.2f}"` in `{python} hi_c.title()`. Those are not small differences in an elasticity. Did they help the prediction? The test RMSE moves from `{python} f"{rmse_log:.4f}"` to `{python} f"{rmse_int:.4f}"`. Barely.

That is a common and useful result. Interactions can be real, and worth knowing about, without mattering much for prediction, because most of the listings are in the counties near the middle of the range and the differences in slope only bite for unusually small or large flats. As in Chapter 9: whether a refinement is worth it is a question about the test error, not about whether the coefficients are significant.

### Worked example — what the interaction changes for one flat

Using the interacted model, how much more does a 1,500 square foot two-bedroom rent than a 1,000 square foot two-bedroom, in 2016, in `{python} lo_c.title()` and in `{python} hi_c.title()`? Answer in per cent.

### Solution

```{python}
#| include: false
pair = pd.DataFrame({"sqft": [1000, 1500] * 2, "beds": 2, "year": 2016,
                     "county": [lo_c, lo_c, hi_c, hi_c]})
lp = fit_int.predict(pair).to_numpy()
pct_lo, pct_hi = np.exp(lp[1] - lp[0]) - 1, np.exp(lp[3] - lp[2]) - 1
```

The flat is 50% bigger, so the log size rises by $\log 1.5 = 0.405$. Multiply by each county's elasticity and exponentiate: in `{python} lo_c.title()` the bigger flat rents for `{python} f"{pct_lo:.0%}"` more, in `{python} hi_c.title()` for `{python} f"{pct_hi:.0%}"` more. (The bedrooms, year and county intercepts cancel, because they are the same for both flats within a county.) In the additive model the answer would be `{python} f"{np.exp(elast * np.log(1.5)) - 1:.0%}"` everywhere.

The economist's caution again: these are differences between flats that exist, not the effect of building an extension. Large flats in `{python} hi_c.title()` may be large *houses* with gardens, and the elasticity is carrying the garden.

## Curves: polynomials and splines

```{python}
#| include: false
def age_profile(age):                        # rises steeply, then flattens out
    return 0.9 * (1 - np.exp(-(age - 18) / 12))

def simulate_wages(n, rng):
    age = rng.integers(18, 66, n)
    educ = rng.choice([10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20], n, p=[.08, .30, .22, .25, .11, .04])
    female = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, n)
    mu = (1.0 + 0.085 * educ + age_profile(age)
          - 0.05 * female - 0.006 * female * (age - 18))          # gender gap widens with age
    sd = 0.2 + 0.035 * (educ - 10)                                 # noisier at high educ
    return pd.DataFrame({"age": age, "educ": educ, "female": female,
                         "wage": np.exp(mu + rng.normal(0, sd, n)), "mu": mu, "sd": sd})

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
wages = simulate_wages(3_000, rng)
big_test = simulate_wages(20_000, np.random.default_rng(1))
small = wages.sample(150, random_state=SEED)
floor = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(big_test["sd"] ** 2)))
```

Size enters the rent model as a log, which is already a curve. For some variables no simple transformation will do, and the classic economic example is age. Wages rise steeply in the first decade of a career and then flatten. A straight line in age misses that shape at both ends.

To see what different methods do, it helps to know the truth, so I simulate it, exactly as in the Lecture 13 notebook: 3,000 CPS-style workers whose log wage depends on schooling, sex and a known age profile, plus noise. Because the data are made up, we know the best possible prediction for every worker, and we know that even that prediction would miss by an RMSE of `{python} f"{floor:.3f}"` log points, the **irreducible error**.

The trick that bends a linear regression is to replace `age` with a few new columns built from age, and run ordinary OLS on those. The model is still linear in its coefficients; only the columns are curved. Two ways to build the columns:

- A **polynomial** adds $\text{age}^2, \text{age}^3, \dots$. Simple, but every term affects the fit at every age, so a few points at one end can swing the whole curve.
- A **spline** cuts the range of age at a few **knots** and fits a separate smooth cubic piece between each pair, glued together so that there are no kinks. Each piece answers mainly to the data near it. A **natural** spline is also forced to be a straight line beyond the outer knots, so it does not fly off at the edges.

In `statsmodels` formulas, `cr(age, df=6)` is a natural spline that uses six columns, and `bs(age, df=6)` is an ordinary cubic **B-spline**. The `df` (degrees of freedom) is the number of columns: more df, more wiggle.

```{python}
#| include: false
grid = pd.DataFrame({"age": np.linspace(18, 65, 300), "educ": 14, "female": 0})
poly10 = " + ".join(f"I(((age - 40) / 15)**{p})" for p in range(1, 11))
specs = {"linear in age": "np.log(wage) ~ educ + female + age",
         "quadratic": "np.log(wage) ~ educ + female + age + I(age**2)",
         "degree-10 polynomial": f"np.log(wage) ~ educ + female + {poly10}",
         "natural spline, df = 6": "np.log(wage) ~ educ + female + cr(age, df=6, constraints='center')"}
fits_small = {k: smf.ols(f, data=small).fit() for k, f in specs.items()}
curve_rmse = pd.DataFrame({k: {"coefficients": len(m.params),
                               "train RMSE": rmse(np.log(small["wage"]), m.predict(small)),
                               "test RMSE": rmse(np.log(big_test["wage"]), m.predict(big_test))}
                           for k, m in fits_small.items()}).T
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Four fits to the age profile, from 150 simulated workers."
truth = 1.0 + 0.085 * 14 + age_profile(grid["age"])
adj = (np.log(small["wage"]) - 0.085 * (small["educ"] - 14)
       + (0.05 + 0.006 * (small["age"] - 18)) * small["female"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(small["age"], adj, s=10, color=GREY, alpha=0.5, label="workers (adjusted to 14 yrs educ, men)")
ax.plot(grid["age"], truth, color="black", ls="--", lw=2, label="truth")
for k, c in zip(["linear in age", "degree-10 polynomial", "natural spline, df = 6"], [BLUE, "#e69f00", GARNET]):
    ax.plot(grid["age"], fits_small[k].predict(grid), color=c, lw=2.2, label=k)
ax.set(xlabel="Age", ylabel="log hourly wage", ylim=(1.6, 4.4),
       title="A polynomial chases noise at the edges; a spline does not")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); plt.show()
```

With only 150 workers the differences are stark. The straight line misses the steep early rise. The degree-10 polynomial follows the noise near 18 and 65, where there are few workers to hold it down. The natural spline tracks the truth closely with six columns. Scored on 20,000 fresh simulated workers:

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(curve_rmse.round(3).to_string(formatters={"coefficients": "{:.0f}".format}))
```

The degree-10 polynomial has the lowest *training* RMSE of the four and a worse *test* RMSE than the spline. You have seen that pattern before, with $k = 1$ in Chapter 9: flexibility that buys a better fit to the training data and pays for it on new data. The spline gets the benefit of bending for little of the cost. Here the humble quadratic does as well, because over ages 18 to 65 the true profile happens to be close to a parabola; the spline did not need to be told that, which is the point of it. Every test RMSE is above the floor of `{python} f"{floor:.3f}"`, as it must be.

scikit-learn has the same tool as a pipeline step, `SplineTransformer`, which we will use in the In Python section:

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer
spline_age = SplineTransformer(n_knots=5, degree=3, extrapolation="linear")
```

`extrapolation="linear"` gives the natural-spline behaviour beyond the outer knots.

### Worked example — predicting outside the data

The simulated workers are aged 18 to 65. A pension office asks for a predicted wage at age 70. What do the degree-10 polynomial and the natural spline (both fitted to the 150 workers) predict, compared with the truth, for a man with 14 years of schooling?

### Solution

```{python}
#| include: false
x70 = pd.DataFrame({"age": [70], "educ": [14], "female": [0]})
p70_poly = float(fits_small["degree-10 polynomial"].predict(x70).iloc[0])
p70_spl = float(fits_small["natural spline, df = 6"].predict(x70).iloc[0])
t70 = 1.0 + 0.085 * 14 + age_profile(70)
```

In log points, the truth is `{python} f"{t70:.2f}"`, the natural spline predicts `{python} f"{p70_spl:.2f}"` and the polynomial `{python} f"{p70_poly:.2f}"`. In dollars an hour (ignoring smearing), that is \$`{python} f"{np.exp(t70):.0f}"`, \$`{python} f"{np.exp(p70_spl):.0f}"` and \$`{python} f"{np.exp(p70_poly):,.0f}"`.

The spline continues in a straight line from its last knot, which is a modest and sensible guess. The polynomial's tenth-power term, which was held in check inside the data, takes over the moment you leave it. Neither model has *seen* a 70-year-old, and the honest answer to the pension office is that no model fitted to these data can tell them much. But if you must extrapolate, a curve that is linear at the edges is the less dangerous one. (A B-spline from `bs()` cannot extrapolate at all: it is simply undefined outside the range it was built on, unless you set its bounds by hand.)

## Learning curves

```{python}
#| include: false
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, ShuffleSplit

pool = simulate_wages(6_000, np.random.default_rng(7))
Xw, yw = pool[["age", "educ", "female"]], np.log(pool["wage"])
stiff = LinearRegression()
bendy = make_pipeline(make_column_transformer((SplineTransformer(n_knots=12), ["age"]), remainder="passthrough"),
                      PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False), LinearRegression())
n_bendy = bendy.fit(Xw, yw)[:-1].transform(Xw.head()).shape[1]
sizes = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 5000]
lc = {}
for name, m in [("stiff", stiff), ("bendy", bendy)]:
    n_, tr_, va_ = learning_curve(m, Xw, yw, train_sizes=sizes, cv=ShuffleSplit(20, test_size=1000, random_state=SEED),
                                  scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    lc[name] = pd.DataFrame({"train": -np.median(tr_, 1), "valid": -np.median(va_, 1)}, index=n_)
splits = ShuffleSplit(20, test_size=1000, random_state=SEED).split(Xw)
floor_lc = float(np.median([rmse(yw.iloc[va], pool["mu"].iloc[va]) for _, va in splits]))   # the truth's own error
```

How do you know whether a model needs more flexibility, less flexibility, or more data? A **learning curve** answers that. Train the model on a small sample, then a larger one, then larger still, and at each size record two numbers: the error on the rows it was trained on, and the error on held-out validation rows. Plot both against the size of the training set.

Here are learning curves for two models of the simulated wages. The **stiff** model is a plain linear regression on age, schooling and sex: three slopes. The **bendy** model puts a 12-knot spline on age and then adds every square and pairwise product of the resulting columns, `{python} n_bendy` columns in all. Each point is the median over 20 random splits, each with 1,000 validation workers.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Learning curves for a stiff and a bendy model of the simulated wages."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6), sharey=True)
for a, name, ttl in zip(ax, ["stiff", "bendy"], ["Stiff: linear in age (high bias)", f"Bendy: {n_bendy} columns (high variance)"]):
    a.plot(lc[name].index, lc[name]["train"], "o-", color=GREY, lw=2, label="training error")
    a.plot(lc[name].index, lc[name]["valid"], "o-", color=GARNET, lw=2, label="validation error")
    a.axhline(floor_lc, color="black", ls=":", lw=1, label="irreducible error")
    a.set(xscale="log", xlabel="Training workers (log scale)", title=ttl, ylim=(0.25, 0.6))
ax[0].set_ylabel("RMSE (log wage)"); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Read the two shapes.

**The stiff model (left) has high bias.** Training and validation error are close together even at 100 workers, and from then on they sit side by side on a plateau at about `{python} f"{lc['stiff']['valid'].iloc[-1]:.3f}"`, above the irreducible error of `{python} f"{floor_lc:.3f}"` (the RMSE that the true average wage itself scores on the same validation workers). More data does nothing: the model has learned all a straight line can learn. The gap between the plateau and the floor is the price of the wrong shape. The cure is a more flexible model, not a bigger sample.

**The bendy model (right) has high variance.** With 100 workers its training error is far below the floor (off the bottom of the chart) and its validation error is enormous (`{python} f"{lc['bendy']['valid'].iloc[0]:.2f}"`, off the top): it is memorising. As the sample grows the gap closes, and by `{python} f"{lc['bendy'].index[-1]:,}"` workers its validation error is `{python} f"{lc['bendy']['valid'].iloc[-1]:.3f}"`, *below* the stiff model's and close to the floor. More data is exactly what this model needed. If you cannot get more data, the cure is to restrain the model: fewer columns, or the penalties of Chapter 11.

> A big gap between training and validation error means variance: get more data or simplify. Two curves that have met at a level you are unhappy with means bias: get a better model or better features.

### Worked example — diagnosing the rent model

Draw the learning curve for the log rent model of this chapter, using 5-fold cross-validation on the training listings at sizes from 500 to the full training set. What does it say the housing office should do next: collect more listings, or improve the model?

### Solution

```{python}
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
rent_model = make_pipeline(ColumnTransformer([
    ("size", FunctionTransformer(np.log), ["sqft"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["beds", "county", "year"])]),
    LinearRegression())
n_r, tr_r, va_r = learning_curve(rent_model, train, train["log_price"], cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
                                 train_sizes=[500, 2_000, 8_000, 20_000, int(0.8 * len(train))],
                                 scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
lc_rent = pd.DataFrame({"train": -tr_r.mean(1), "valid": -va_r.mean(1)}, index=n_r).round(3)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(lc_rent.to_string())
```

This is the stiff shape. By about 2,000 listings, training and validation error have met at about `{python} f"{lc_rent['valid'].iloc[-1]:.2f}"`, and the next `{python} f"{lc_rent.index[-1] - 2000:,}"` listings move the validation error by `{python} f"{lc_rent['valid'].iloc[1] - lc_rent['valid'].iloc[-1]:.3f}"`. The model is bias-limited. Another 50,000 ads would not help; better features would. Neighbourhood instead of county is the obvious first step (Exercise 4), and the more flexible models of Chapters 14 and 15 are the next. That is a useful thing to know before anyone spends money on data.

## Confidence intervals and prediction intervals

```{python}
#| include: false
x0 = pd.DataFrame({"sqft": [1000], "beds": [2], "county": ["san francisco"], "year": [2016]})
sf0 = fit.get_prediction(x0).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
ci_lo, ci_hi = np.exp(sf0["mean_ci_lower"].iloc[0]), np.exp(sf0["mean_ci_upper"].iloc[0])
pi_lo, pi_hi = np.exp(sf0["obs_ci_lower"].iloc[0]), np.exp(sf0["obs_ci_upper"].iloc[0])
mid0 = np.exp(sf0["mean"].iloc[0])
pi_all = fit.get_prediction(test).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
covered = ((test["log_price"].to_numpy() >= pi_all["obs_ci_lower"].to_numpy())
           & (test["log_price"].to_numpy() <= pi_all["obs_ci_upper"].to_numpy()))
cov_all = covered.mean()
cov_cty = pd.Series(covered, index=test.index).groupby(test["county"]).mean().sort_values()
```

A prediction without a range is half an answer. But there are two different ranges, answering two different questions, and mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in applied work.

Take a 1,000 square foot two-bedroom in San Francisco in 2016. The model's central prediction is \$`{python} usd(mid0)` a month (in this section I exponentiate without smearing, to keep the two intervals on the same footing).

- The **confidence interval** answers: *what is the average rent of all flats like this one?* We do not know the coefficients exactly, so we do not know the average exactly. With `{python} f"{len(train):,}"` listings we know it rather well: the 95% interval is \$`{python} usd(ci_lo)` to \$`{python} usd(ci_hi)`.
- The **prediction interval** answers: *what will this particular flat rent for?* That adds the flat's own luck, everything about it the model does not see. The 95% interval is \$`{python} usd(pi_lo)` to \$`{python} usd(pi_hi)`.

`statsmodels` gives both; the confidence interval is `mean_ci_lower` and `mean_ci_upper`, the prediction interval `obs_ci_lower` and `obs_ci_upper`:

```python
fit.get_prediction(x0).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
```

The difference in width is not a detail. The confidence interval shrinks towards zero as the sample grows: with a million listings we would know the average rent of such flats almost exactly. The prediction interval does not shrink below the noise. No amount of data tells you whether *this* flat has a view.

Are the prediction intervals honest? Check them the way Chapter 8 checked confidence intervals, by **coverage**: the share of test listings whose actual log rent falls inside their own 95% interval. Overall it is `{python} f"{cov_all:.1%}"`, almost exactly right. By county it runs from `{python} f"{cov_cty.iloc[0]:.1%}"` in `{python} cov_cty.index[0].title()` to `{python} f"{cov_cty.iloc[-1]:.1%}"` in `{python} cov_cty.index[-1].title()`. The interval uses one noise level for every flat, and rents in `{python} cov_cty.index[0].title()` are harder to predict than elsewhere, so the interval is too narrow there and too wide where rents are steadier.

### Worked example — which interval for whom?

Two people ask the housing office about 1,000 square foot two-bedrooms in San Francisco. A tenant wants to know what she should expect to pay for one. The office's budget officer wants to know what 3,000 such vouchers will cost in total. Which interval does each need?

### Solution

The tenant needs the **prediction interval**, \$`{python} usd(pi_lo)` to \$`{python} usd(pi_hi)`. She will rent one flat, with its own luck. Telling her \$`{python} usd(ci_lo)` to \$`{python} usd(ci_hi)` would badly overstate how sure anyone can be.

The budget officer is closer to the **confidence interval**. Over 3,000 flats the individual lucks largely average out (some flats are dearer than predicted, some cheaper), and what remains is uncertainty about the average. Even so, I would give her the average in *dollars*, which means smearing, since a sum of exponentiated log predictions is too low for exactly the reason the earlier section described. And the confidence interval assumes that these 3,000 flats are like the listings in the data, which is the assumption to check first.

## In Python

The whole chapter's model in one runnable place: a log rent model with splines in size and year, neighbourhood dummies, smearing back to dollars, and a test score in dollars.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer, OneHotEncoder, FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
SEED = 368

path = Path("../data/rent.csv")                       # download once, then reuse
if not path.exists():
    path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    pd.read_csv(URL).to_csv(path, index=False)
rent = pd.read_csv(path)
d = (rent.dropna(subset=["beds", "sqft", "county"])
         .query("room_in_apt == 0 and beds <= 5 and 200 <= sqft <= 5000 and 500 <= price <= 15000"))
X, y = d[["sqft", "beds", "year", "county", "nhood"]], np.log(d["price"])
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED)
```

Size gets a log and then a spline; year gets a spline; the categories are one-hot encoded, with rare neighbourhoods lumped together as in Chapter 9.

```{python}
log_spline = make_pipeline(FunctionTransformer(np.log), SplineTransformer(n_knots=6, extrapolation="linear"))
prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("size", log_spline, ["sqft"]),
    ("year", SplineTransformer(n_knots=5, extrapolation="linear"), ["year"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=50), ["beds", "county", "nhood"])])
model = make_pipeline(prep, LinearRegression())

cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
cv_log = -cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(f"CV RMSE: {cv_log.mean():.3f} log points")
```

Fit once on all the training data, smear, and score once on the test set, in dollars.

```{python}
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
smear = np.mean(np.exp(y_train - model.predict(X_train)))
pred = smear * np.exp(model.predict(X_test))
print(f"smearing factor {smear:.4f}")
print(f"Test RMSE: ${root_mean_squared_error(np.exp(y_test), pred):,.0f} a month; "
      f"{root_mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test)):.3f} log points")
```

```{python}
#| include: false
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
final_dollars = root_mean_squared_error(np.exp(y_test), pred)
num9, cat9 = ["sqft", "beds", "baths", "year"], ["county", "nhood"]
knn9 = make_pipeline(ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), num9),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=50), cat9)]),
    KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=10)).fit(train[num9 + cat9], train["price"])
knn_dollars = root_mean_squared_error(test["price"], knn9.predict(test[num9 + cat9]))
```

The test RMSE in dollars, \$`{python} usd(final_dollars)`, compares with \$`{python} usd(r_smear)` for the county model earlier in the chapter. For a benchmark, Chapter 9's nearest-neighbours model with $k = 10$, fitted to the same training listings, misses the same test listings by \$`{python} usd(knn_dollars)`. `{python} "The linear model is close behind it" if final_dollars > knn_dollars else "The linear model beats it"`, and unlike nearest neighbours it can be written down on a page.

## What goes wrong

**Exponentiating log predictions and calling them dollars.** $e^{\hat y}$ estimates something close to the median, not the mean, so naive predictions are too low on average: here by `{python} f"{1 - pred_naive.mean() / test['price'].mean():.1%}"`. For a budget that is real money. Multiply by the smearing factor.

**Raw features in gradient descent.** Unscaled features turn the bowl into a narrow valley and force a tiny learning rate. Standardise first. And if the training loss goes *up* as you train, the learning rate is too big; halve it.

**Trusting a polynomial at the edges.** High-degree polynomials are worst exactly where the data are thinnest, and they are catastrophic outside the data: our degree-10 fit predicts a 70-year-old earns \$`{python} f"{np.exp(p70_poly):,.0f}"` an hour. Use a natural spline, and be suspicious of any prediction outside the range of the training data.

**Collecting more data for a bias-limited model.** If training and validation error have already met, more rows will not move either. Draw the learning curve before you buy data.

**Reporting a confidence interval when someone needs a prediction interval.** A tenant, a borrower or a benefit claimant is one case, with one case's luck. The confidence interval for the mean is far too narrow for them.

**Reading the predictor as an estimator.** The size elasticity of `{python} f"{elast:.2f}"` is a good predictive weight. It is not the value of an extension, and the county-by-county elasticities are not the value of space in each county. If the decision depends on $\hat\beta$, Chapter 9's warning applies.

## Exercises

1. A model of log wages has a test RMSE of 0.40. A model of wages in dollars has a test RMSE of \$9.50. Can you tell which is better from these two numbers? What would you compute to compare them?

2. Write mini-batch gradient descent for the three-feature rent model (log size, bedrooms, year, standardised). Try batch sizes of 1, 64 and 4,096 with a learning rate of 0.01 for two epochs. How far is each from the normal-equation coefficients, and how many updates did each take?

3. Smearing uses one factor for every flat. Compute the smearing factor separately for each county from the training residuals of the log model, and compare the average predicted rent (naive, single-factor smearing, county smearing) with the average actual rent in each county on the test set. Where does a single factor do worst?

4. Replace `C(county)` with neighbourhood dummies in the log model (lumping neighbourhoods with fewer than 50 training listings into "other", using training counts only). How much does the test RMSE fall? Redraw the learning curve: is the model still bias-limited?

5. Without computing anything: if the training set were ten times as large, what would happen to the width of the confidence interval and of the prediction interval for the San Francisco flat? Why?

6. Refit the log model with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (`cov_type="HC1"`) and recompute the coverage of the 95% prediction intervals by county. Did it fix the problem in `{python} cov_cty.index[0].title()`? Explain why or why not.

7. A landlord in `{python} hi_c.title()` reads that the size elasticity there is `{python} f"{el.loc[hi_c]:.2f}"` and concludes that a 20% extension will raise her rent by about `{python} f"{20 * el.loc[hi_c]:.0f}"`%. What would you tell her?

### Answers

**1.** No. The first is in log points, the second in dollars, so they are not in the same units. Put them on the same scale: convert the log model's predictions to dollars (with smearing) and compute its RMSE in dollars on the same test set, or take logs of the dollar model's predictions (where positive) and compute its RMSE in log points. Then decide which scale matches the decision. This chapter compared the rent models in dollars because the vouchers are paid in dollars.

**2.**

```{python}
def minibatch(batch, eta=0.01, epochs=2, seed=SEED):
    rng, b, steps = np.random.default_rng(seed), np.zeros(X3.shape[1]), 0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for idx in np.array_split(rng.permutation(len(y3)), max(len(y3) // batch, 1)):
            b = b - eta * 2 / len(idx) * X3[idx].T @ (X3[idx] @ b - y3[idx])
            steps += 1
    return np.abs(b - b_exact).max(), steps
mb = pd.DataFrame({bs: minibatch(bs) for bs in [1, 64, 4096]}, index=["max gap", "updates"]).T
print(mb.to_string(formatters={"max gap": "{:.4f}".format, "updates": "{:,.0f}".format}))
```

With batches of one row (pure SGD), `{python} f"{mb.loc[1, 'updates']:,.0f}"` updates get within `{python} f"{mb.loc[1, 'max gap']:.3f}"`: close, but each step is noisy, so it never settles exactly. Batches of 64 take `{python} f"{mb.loc[64, 'updates']:,.0f}"` updates and land within `{python} f"{mb.loc[64, 'max gap']:.4f}"`. Batches of 4,096 take only `{python} f"{mb.loc[4096, 'updates']:,.0f}"` updates, which at this learning rate is not enough to reach the bottom (`{python} f"{mb.loc[4096, 'max gap']:.3f}"` off). Larger batches give better steps, but fewer of them per epoch; with large batches you can afford a larger learning rate.

**3.**

```{python}
res = train.assign(e=np.exp(fit.resid))
smear_cty = res.groupby("county")["e"].mean()
chk = test.assign(naive=pred_naive, single=pred_smear,
                  by_county=pred_naive * test["county"].map(smear_cty).to_numpy())
gap = chk.groupby("county")[["price", "naive", "single", "by_county"]].mean()
gap_pct = gap[["naive", "single", "by_county"]].div(gap["price"], axis=0) - 1
print(gap_pct.round(3).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| include: false
worst = gap_pct["single"].abs().idxmax()
n_worst = int((test["county"] == worst).sum())
sf_single, sf_cty = gap_pct.loc["san francisco", "single"], gap_pct.loc["san francisco", "by_county"]
```

Naive predictions are too low, or at best about right, in every county. A single smearing factor fixes most of that. The worst county after smearing is `{python} worst.title()` (`{python} f"{gap_pct.loc[worst, 'single']:+.1%}"`), and a county-specific factor barely helps there (`{python} f"{gap_pct.loc[worst, 'by_county']:+.1%}"`). That is not a smearing problem: `{python} worst.title()` has only `{python} n_worst` test listings, and a few expensive houses among them can move the average by several per cent. Where county smearing clearly helps is San Francisco, from `{python} f"{sf_single:+.1%}"` to `{python} f"{sf_cty:+.1%}"`. San Francisco is where the residuals are most spread out, the same heteroskedasticity that made the prediction intervals too narrow there. When the noise differs across groups, smearing by group is a cheap improvement; just check that the groups are big enough for their averages to mean something.

**4.**

```{python}
keep = train["nhood"].value_counts().loc[lambda s: s >= 50].index
tr4, te4 = (df_.assign(nh=df_["nhood"].where(df_["nhood"].isin(keep), "other")) for df_ in (train, test))
fit_nh = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(sqft) + C(beds) + C(nh) + C(year)", data=tr4).fit()
rmse_nh = rmse(te4["log_price"], fit_nh.predict(te4))
rent_nh = make_pipeline(ColumnTransformer([
    ("size", FunctionTransformer(np.log), ["sqft"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=50), ["beds", "nhood", "year"])]),
    LinearRegression())
n4, tr_4, va_4 = learning_curve(rent_nh, train, train["log_price"], cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
                                train_sizes=[2_000, 8_000, int(0.8 * len(train))], scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(round(rmse_nh, 4), (-tr_4.mean(1)).round(3), (-va_4.mean(1)).round(3))
```

Neighbourhoods cut the test RMSE from `{python} f"{rmse_log:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{rmse_nh:.3f}"` log points: location within a county matters a great deal. The learning curve is more interesting than before. Training and validation error still meet at every size, so there is no sign of variance. But the validation error now keeps falling as the data grow, from `{python} f"{-va_4.mean(1)[0]:.3f}"` at 2,000 listings to `{python} f"{-va_4.mean(1)[-1]:.3f}"` at full size. The reason is `min_frequency=50`: in a small sample most neighbourhoods are too rare to get their own dummy and are lumped into "other"; in a large one they earn their own. More data helps this model, through the features it lets the model use. A learning curve tells you about a model *and* its features together.

**5.** The confidence interval would shrink, roughly by a factor of $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$, because it measures uncertainty about the coefficients, and that falls with the sample size. The prediction interval would hardly change. Most of its width is the noise in individual rents, which does not depend on how many flats we have seen; only the small part that comes from uncertainty about the coefficients would shrink.

**6.**

```{python}
fit_hc = smf.ols(FORMULA, data=train).fit(cov_type="HC1")
pi_hc = fit_hc.get_prediction(test).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
cov_hc = ((test["log_price"].to_numpy() >= pi_hc["obs_ci_lower"].to_numpy())
          & (test["log_price"].to_numpy() <= pi_hc["obs_ci_upper"].to_numpy()))
cov_hc_cty = pd.Series(cov_hc, index=test.index).groupby(test["county"]).mean()
print(pd.DataFrame({"classical": cov_cty, "HC1": cov_hc_cty}).round(3).to_string())
```

It did not. Not a single listing changed sides: coverage in `{python} cov_cty.index[0].title()` is `{python} f"{cov_hc_cty.loc[cov_cty.index[0]]:.1%}"` either way. Robust standard errors fix the *coefficients'* uncertainty when the noise varies. But the prediction interval is mostly the noise itself, and it still uses one noise level for every flat. To fix it you have to model the noise: estimate how the spread of residuals varies by county (or with the features), or use quantile regression or conformal prediction, which build the interval from held-out errors directly.

**7.** That the number cannot carry that weight. `{python} f"{el.loc[hi_c]:.2f}"` describes how rents differ between bigger and smaller flats that exist in `{python} hi_c.title()`, and bigger flats there differ in many ways besides size: more of them are houses, with gardens and parking. An extension adds square feet and nothing else. The prediction model is useful for pricing a flat like the ones in the data; it is not an estimate of what *changing* a flat would do. That is a $\hat\beta$ question, and it needs a research design, such as comparing the same units before and after renovations.

## Economics reading

A rent regression has a long history in economics under another name. These papers explain what its coefficients mean, why Bay Area rents are so high, and how new data are changing the measurement of cities.

**Rosen, S. (1974). "Hedonic Prices and Implicit Markets: Product Differentiation in Pure Competition." *Journal of Political Economy* 82(1): 34–55.** [doi.org/10.1086/260169](https://doi.org/10.1086/260169)

The theory behind every regression of a price on product characteristics. Rosen treats a flat (or a car, or a job) as a bundle of attributes and asks what the slope of price with respect to one attribute means. His answer is that the price schedule traces out an equilibrium in which buyers with different tastes are matched with sellers who can supply different bundles. The slope at a point tells you what the marginal buyer there pays for a little more, not what any one household would pay, and not a demand curve.

*Think about:* the chapter's size elasticity is a slope of this kind. Is it what a particular tenant would pay for 100 more square feet? What would happen to the slope if a wave of families with children moved into the Bay Area, and why does Rosen's view make the predictive model and the economic interpretation different things?

**Glaeser, E. & Gyourko, J. (2018). "The Economic Implications of Housing Supply." *Journal of Economic Perspectives* 32(1): 3–30.** [doi.org/10.1257/jep.32.1.3](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.32.1.3)

The authors compare house prices with the cost of building, and find that in most of the United States homes sell for about what they cost to build. In a few coastal metropolitan areas, the San Francisco Bay Area among them, prices are far above construction cost. They attribute the gap mainly to restrictions on building, and argue that it keeps workers out of the most productive places, with costs for the whole economy.

*Think about:* the county effects in the chapter's model capture how much more a similar flat rents for in San Francisco than elsewhere. What supply-side reasons could make that effect so large, and could the prediction model tell you whether allowing more construction would lower rents? What kind of evidence would?

**Glaeser, E. L., Kominers, S. D., Luca, M. & Naik, N. (2018). "Big Data and Big Cities: The Promises and Limitations of Improved Measures of Urban Life." *Economic Inquiry* 56(1): 114–137.** [doi.org/10.1111/ecin.12364](https://doi.org/10.1111/ecin.12364)

The authors show how online and image data can measure cities in ways surveys cannot: for example, predicting the income of a neighbourhood from Street View images, or tracking local businesses from online reviews. They are equally clear about the limits: the measures are predictions, they can miss places that are poorly covered online, and they do not by themselves answer causal questions.

*Think about:* suppose you added features built from street images to the rent model. What would the model probably learn from them, and what would go wrong if landlords could see which visible features raise the voucher?

**Reading.** Géron, ch. 4, for the normal equation, the three flavours of gradient descent, polynomial regression and learning curves. ISLP (James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani & Taylor 2023), ch. 3 and ch. 7, for linear regression as prediction and for polynomials, splines and generalised additive models. Duan (1983), "Smearing Estimate: A Nonparametric Retransformation Method", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 78(383), for smearing.
